questions.title: Copy without consuming
questions.prompt: A game copies an ammo count from one register into another. What happens to the original register?
options: It keeps its value while the destination receives a copy
It becomes zero once the destination receives the count
It becomes an address pointing at the destination register
It loses its type until the game reads the ammo field again
questions.explanation: An ordinary register copy writes the destination without consuming or clearing the source. The same value can remain in both registers.

questions.title: Calculate before reading
questions.prompt: Code calculates the address of a player field but performs no load there. What has it learned?
options: A candidate location, without learning the field value yet
The field value, because every address calculation reads it
The object lifetime, because a calculated address is valid
The source variable name, because field offsets encode names
questions.explanation: Address arithmetic calculates where bytes would be. A separate memory access is needed to learn their contents, and validity and lifetime still require evidence.

questions.title: Step through records
questions.prompt: A player record is 24 bytes wide and health is eight bytes into it. How should the next player be reached?
options: Advance the record base by 24, then add the field offset
Advance the record base by eight, then reuse the old value
Advance the record base by four, since health has four bytes
Advance the record base by one, because the index is a count
questions.explanation: Record stride and field width are different. Each next record begins 24 bytes later; its health field is still eight bytes into that record.

questions.title: Separate two overflow questions
questions.prompt: A 32-bit value holding all one bits receives one more. As unsigned it exceeds its range; as signed it is minus one plus one. Which interpretation fits?
options: Unsigned carry occurs, while this signed sum still fits
Signed overflow occurs, while this unsigned sum still fits
Both sums exceed their ranges because the stored bits wrap
Neither sum exceeds its range because the result is zero
questions.explanation: The stored result is zero. CF reports the unsigned carry beyond 32 bits; signed minus one plus one equals zero and does not set signed overflow.

questions.title: Interpret the signed boundary
questions.prompt: Adding one to the largest positive signed 32-bit value sets signed overflow but no unsigned carry. Why?
options: The signed sum is too large, but the unsigned sum fits
The unsigned sum is too large, but the signed sum fits
A positive input disables carry until a negative one arrives
The result width grows automatically to keep the sum exact
questions.explanation: The same bits have different ranges under signed and unsigned interpretations. OF and CF report those separate boundary questions.

questions.title: Know who wrote a flag
questions.prompt: A count increases by one using an operation that preserves the carry flag. Carry was already set. What does carry now prove about this increase?
options: Nothing new; it still records the earlier flag producer
That this increase overflowed the unsigned count exactly
That this increase overflowed the signed count exactly
That this increase stored zero in the destination register
questions.explanation: A preserved flag is old information. The increment may update zero, sign, and overflow flags, but its preserved carry is not a fresh carry result.

questions.title: Read the chosen width
questions.prompt: An instruction stores one byte into a four-byte game field. What should you check before treating the whole field as replaced?
options: Which remaining bytes were left unchanged by that store
Which register became four times wider after that store
Which field name was encoded inside the stored byte value
Which page acquired execution permission after that store
questions.explanation: A one-byte store replaces only its selected byte. The remaining bytes can keep older contents, so the complete four-byte value may differ from a simple reading of the new byte.

questions.title: Keep the full product in mind
questions.prompt: Signed multiplication keeps only the low 32 bits and reports that the exact product did not fit. What is safe to conclude?
options: The stored bits are truncated, so the reward needs handling
The stored bits are exact, because multiplication never wraps
The source field was erased, because multiplication consumes it
The zero flag proves success, because every product sets it
questions.explanation: A low-width product can differ from the exact mathematical signed result. Overflow reporting needs handling; undefined result flags cannot establish success.

questions.title: Prepare the whole dividend
questions.prompt: A signed divide instruction reads a double-width dividend from two registers. The low register is correct but the high one is stale. What is the problem?
options: The combined dividend can differ from the intended value
The stale high register is ignored for every small divisor
The quotient is correct but its decimal display is reversed
The divisor automatically replaces the stale high register
questions.explanation: The implicit high half is part of the dividend. Preparing only the low register is insufficient; signed division normally needs the appropriate sign extension.

questions.title: Understand rounding toward zero
questions.prompt: A signed coin adjustment of minus seven is divided by three using truncation toward zero. What quotient and remainder result?
options: Quotient minus two, with a remainder of minus one
Quotient minus three, with a remainder of positive two
Quotient positive two, with a remainder of positive one
Quotient minus one, with a remainder of positive four
questions.explanation: Truncation toward zero gives minus two. The remainder makes the identity hold: minus seven equals minus two times three plus minus one.

questions.title: Guard division before it runs
questions.prompt: A sharing rule has a valid coin total but zero participants. What should a division-based implementation do?
options: Handle the zero-participant case before attempting division
Divide first and inspect the carry flag for the missing result
Divide first and treat the previous quotient as the new share
Use the zero divisor as a request to divide the total by one
questions.explanation: Integer division by zero raises a divide-error exception. The game rule must define and guard the zero-participant case before invoking the instruction.

questions.title: Check the quotient range
questions.prompt: A divisor is nonzero, but the exact signed quotient cannot fit the destination register. Is the divide automatically safe?
options: No; a quotient-range failure can raise divide error as well
Yes; every nonzero divisor guarantees that the quotient fits
Yes; the processor silently returns a wider register result
No; the processor always clears both input registers first
questions.explanation: A nonzero divisor removes only one failure case. A quotient that does not fit the instruction result width can also raise divide error.

questions.title: Widen an unsigned field
questions.prompt: An unsigned eight-bit count has all eight bits set. It is widened by filling new high bits with zeros. What is preserved?
options: Its numeric value of 255 in the wider representation
Its numeric value of minus one in the wider representation
Its original memory address as the wider numeric value
Its original bit width while only its variable name changes
questions.explanation: Zero extension preserves the numeric value of an unsigned smaller field. Eight one bits become a wider value with zeros above them, still 255.

questions.title: Widen a signed field
questions.prompt: A signed eight-bit movement delta represents minus one. Why repeat its top bit when widening it?
options: Repeating the sign bit preserves the signed numeric value
Repeating the sign bit turns the delta into an unsigned count
Repeating the sign bit validates the pointer to the game object
Repeating the sign bit preserves only its least significant bit
questions.explanation: Sign extension fills the new high bits with the old sign bit. In two-complement representation this keeps minus one as minus one rather than interpreting it as 255.

questions.title: Separate address from lifetime
questions.prompt: Address arithmetic gives a plausible field location. What additional evidence is needed before reading it?
options: That the mapping and intended object are valid for the access
That the address has the same final digit as the field offset
That a previous run once used an object at the same location
That the instruction calculating it left the zero flag clear
questions.explanation: A plausible location does not establish a live object or accessible mapping. Bounds, lifetime, mapping permissions, and the intended layout still matter.

questions.title: Compare before changing
questions.prompt: A shop checks a gold amount against a cost using a comparison. What changes during that comparison alone?
options: The comparison flags change while the gold value stays put
The gold value changes while the comparison flags stay put
Both gold and price become the subtraction result together
The return address becomes the cost of the selected purchase
questions.explanation: An integer comparison computes subtraction flags and discards the numeric difference. Spending requires a separate write or arithmetic update.

questions.title: Inspect without deleting
questions.prompt: A status word contains several independent bits. You want to inspect one bit while keeping every status value intact. What operation is needed?
options: A temporary masked comparison that discards its bit result
A masked store that keeps only the selected status bit alive
A complement of the entire status word before inspecting it
A shift that permanently removes every bit below the target
questions.explanation: A masked test can update flags from a temporary AND without changing the original status word. A stored AND would clear unselected bits.

questions.title: Choose the intended ordering
questions.prompt: The same 32 bits represent minus one as signed and a very large value as unsigned. Can comparisons with a small positive number choose opposite paths?
options: Yes; signed and unsigned ordering interpret those bits differently
No; the flags store the source language type along with each result
No; all ordering comparisons must use the same highest-bit test
Yes; only because the comparison also rewrites the original value
questions.explanation: A signed less-than condition uses sign and overflow; unsigned below uses borrow. Their different interpretations can produce opposite ordering for identical operand bits.

questions.title: Keep comparison results live
questions.prompt: A comparison is followed by arithmetic before its conditional branch. What needs checking?
options: Whether the arithmetic replaced flags that the branch will read
Whether the branch restored the original source-code field names
Whether the arithmetic resized the branch into a new CPU register
Whether the comparison automatically froze all following flags
questions.explanation: Flags are current processor state, not a permanent attachment to the earlier comparison. A later arithmetic instruction can replace the condition that the branch reads.

questions.title: Distinguish a jump from a call
questions.prompt: A control transfer enters a helper without saving a return address. Which expectation is unsafe?
options: Expecting an ordinary return to know where the transfer came from
Expecting the instruction pointer to change to the helper location
Expecting the helper to execute instructions at its own location
Expecting earlier game memory to remain available in the process
questions.explanation: An ordinary jump does not save a continuation. A return consumes an existing stack address; the surrounding code must deliberately establish it.

questions.title: Save the correct continuation
questions.prompt: An ordinary near call saves a return address. Which point should that address identify?
options: The instruction immediately after the call in the caller
The first instruction of the helper that was just entered
The most recent memory field read before the call occurred
The end of the entire program regardless of which helper ran
questions.explanation: The saved continuation lets the helper return to the next instruction in its caller. It is neither a pointer to the helper start nor a game-data field.

questions.title: Know who made the result
questions.prompt: A helper calculates a number in a result register and then returns. Which action actually produced the numeric result?
options: The helper calculation, with the calling convention choosing its register
The return instruction, which computes a new number from the stack bytes
The call instruction, which always initializes all result registers to zero
The saved address, which changes into the numeric result during the return
questions.explanation: Return transfers control using the saved address. The helper instructions produced the result; the calling convention explains where the caller expects it.

questions.title: Reverse temporary saves
questions.prompt: Code saves two registers on a last-in, first-out stack. How should it restore those saved values?
options: Restore the last saved register first, then the earlier one
Restore the first saved register first, then the later one
Restore both into whichever register currently contains zero
Restore only one because both saves share one stack address
questions.explanation: The last pushed value is at the top. Reversing the save order restores the intended registers and avoids leaving an extra slot above the return address.

questions.title: Distinguish active storage from leftovers
questions.prompt: A stack value is popped, but inspecting the old memory slot still shows its bytes. What does that mean?
options: The bytes can remain even though that slot is no longer active
The pop failed because successful removal must erase the bytes
The popped register still borrows the slot instead of holding a value
The return address must have moved into those leftover bytes automatically
questions.explanation: Popping changes the active top and copies the value. It normally does not overwrite the old slot, so leftover bytes alone do not prove live stack data.

questions.title: Handle a zero effective count
questions.prompt: A bit-shift instruction receives an effective count of zero. What happens to the operand and its arithmetic flags?
options: Both keep their prior values rather than producing a new shift result
The operand keeps its value while all arithmetic flags become zero
The operand becomes zero while its earlier arithmetic flags survive
Both become undefined because a shift requires at least one position
questions.explanation: A zero effective shift count preserves the value and flags. For nonzero counts, specific flags change, and overflow is only defined for a one-bit shift.

questions.title: Compare shift and division rounding
questions.prompt: A negative odd integer is shifted right while repeating its sign bit. Why can that differ from signed division by two?
options: The shift rounds downward while signed division truncates toward zero
The shift rounds toward zero while signed division always rounds upward
The shift converts the number into a float before moving any of its bits
The shift uses an unsigned divisor even though the input remains signed
questions.explanation: Arithmetic right shift of a negative odd value rounds toward minus infinity. Signed integer division truncates toward zero, so minus three becomes minus two by shift but minus one by division.

questions.title: Set a state consistently
questions.prompt: A control may request the same enabled state twice. Which bit rule keeps the state enabled on both requests?
options: Set the bit with an OR mask instead of toggling it each time
Toggle the bit with an XOR mask each time the request arrives
Complement the whole word each time the request arrives
Clear the bit with an AND mask before treating it as enabled
questions.explanation: OR with a one-bit mask sets that bit whether it was previously zero or one. XOR toggles it, so two identical requests would undo each other.

questions.title: Read the entire selected width
questions.prompt: A 32-bit word is complemented, but an illustration displays only its four lowest bits. What happens to the unseen high bits?
options: They invert too, because the operation uses the full selected width
They stay unchanged, because unseen bits are outside the bit operation
They become undefined, because the drawing omits their numeric labels
They move into the low four positions before the complement is applied
questions.explanation: The displayed boxes are a partial view. A full-width bitwise complement inverts every selected bit, including the high bits absent from that illustration.

questions.title: Keep following the path
questions.prompt: An instruction performs no data operation and execution advances. Does that prevent the next instruction from spending ammo?
options: No; the next instruction still runs unless another control transfer stops it
Yes; doing no work stops all later writes until the program restarts
No; but it automatically restores any ammo spent by the next instruction
Yes; doing no work is equivalent to returning from the current function
questions.explanation: A no-op does not pause, return, or undo later work. Execution continues to the next instruction, which can still perform the ammo update.

questions.title: Inspect the state before the action
questions.prompt: A deliberate one-byte breakpoint instruction precedes an ammo subtraction. The debugger pauses on its exception. Has the later subtraction executed?
options: No; the saved continuation follows the breakpoint and precedes that action
Yes; breakpoint handling always executes the next instruction before pausing
No; because the breakpoint permanently removed that action from the function
Yes; because a breakpoint is simply a data-neutral instruction with no exception
questions.explanation: The breakpoint transfers through exception handling. In this deliberate breakpoint case, the saved next instruction is after the breakpoint byte, and continuation is a separate debugger decision.

questions.title: Read the low scalar value
questions.prompt: A scalar single-precision operation uses an XMM register. How much of that register holds the numeric value being calculated?
options: One low 32-bit float inside the wider register storage
One 128-bit integer using every bit of the register storage
Four 32-bit floats that must all change on every scalar step
One pointer whose address selects the floating-point format
questions.explanation: Scalar single-precision operations calculate one binary32 value in the low 32 bits. The rest of the 128-bit XMM register still exists and follows that instruction form's rules.

questions.title: Check the exact copy form
questions.prompt: Two legacy scalar float copies have the same low value, but one loads from memory and one copies another XMM register. Why inspect their forms?
options: Their rules for the destination upper bits are different
Their low values must use opposite byte order in memory
Their source values both become zero after a successful copy
Their integer zero flags always disagree after the two copies
questions.explanation: Legacy movss from memory clears destination XMM bits 127:32, while the register copy preserves them. Stores write only the selected four-byte scalar.

questions.title: Keep bits and value separate
questions.prompt: An integer score is needed as a floating-point numeric value. Why is merely copying its four bytes insufficient?
options: Integer and float formats assign different meanings to the same bits
Integer and float formats require different physical memory address sizes
Every integer occupies eight bytes while every float occupies four bytes
A byte copy consumes the score before its new representation can be read
questions.explanation: Numeric conversion constructs a floating-point encoding of the integer's value. A copy instead preserves the integer bit pattern, which usually has a different meaning as a float.

questions.title: Do not read an old carry
questions.prompt: A scalar floating-point multiply is followed by an integer carry branch. What can that branch reveal about this multiplication alone?
options: Nothing reliable; that arithmetic did not make a new integer carry result
Whether the float multiplied past its unsigned 32-bit integer maximum
Whether the float result is zero because carry always becomes its zero test
Whether the float has a fractional part because carry records discarded digits
questions.explanation: Scalar SSE arithmetic uses floating-point control/status in MXCSR and preserves integer comparison flags. An integer carry branch can therefore read an earlier operation's carry.

questions.title: Allow for representable values
questions.prompt: A signed 32-bit integer fits its integer register but becomes slightly different when converted to a single-precision float. What explains this?
options: The float format cannot represent every such integer exactly
The conversion always keeps only the last decimal digit of the input
The integer register lost its low bits before the conversion was selected
The source value was unsigned because positive integers have no signed form
questions.explanation: Binary32 has limited significand precision. Some larger 32-bit integers need rounding even though they fit the integer source register.

questions.title: Know truncation direction
questions.prompt: A float value of minus 2.75 is converted to a signed integer by truncating toward zero. Which value results?
options: Minus two, because the fractional part is discarded toward zero
Minus three, because every negative fraction must round downward
Positive two, because integer conversion removes the sign bit first
Zero, because a negative fractional value has no integer representation
questions.explanation: Truncation toward zero gives minus two for minus 2.75 and two for 2.75. It differs from rounding down on negative values.

questions.title: Know what a masked invalid conversion does
questions.prompt: An out-of-range float-to-integer conversion has its invalid-operation exception masked. What can happen?
options: An indefinite integer is written and floating-point status records invalid
A larger integer register is automatically allocated for the exact answer
The source float is clamped to the largest valid input without reporting it
The zero flag becomes the exact count of missing destination bits afterward
questions.explanation: For the 32-bit cvttss2si form, masked invalid returns the indefinite integer 0x80000000 and records invalid operation in MXCSR. This is not an ordinary valid conversion result.

questions.title: Recognize the exception path
questions.prompt: A numeric conversion encounters invalid input and the corresponding floating-point exception is unmasked. Which expectation is unsafe?
options: Assuming a normal converted integer was produced before the exception path
Expecting exception handling to interrupt the ordinary conversion path
Expecting the caller to define how invalid numeric input should be handled
Expecting the result width and input range to matter when validating the value
questions.explanation: An unmasked invalid-operation condition raises an exception. Code must not assume that the normal conversion result and following store have completed.

questions.title: Validate more than the returned bits
questions.prompt: A conversion output has the same bit pattern as the valid minimum signed integer. Does that pattern alone prove conversion succeeded?
options: No; an invalid masked conversion can return that same indefinite pattern
Yes; the minimum signed integer is reserved exclusively for successful conversion
No; every successful conversion clears all destination bits before returning
Yes; invalid conversions always choose a pattern outside the integer bit width
questions.explanation: The indefinite output of a masked invalid 32-bit conversion is 0x80000000, which also encodes the valid signed minimum. Validation or appropriate status handling is needed to distinguish them.

questions.title: Leave room for unordered values
questions.prompt: A speed field contains NaN and is compared with a numeric limit. Which description is accurate?
options: Its comparison is unordered rather than less, equal, or greater
Its comparison is equal because both values occupy four bytes
Its comparison is less because every NaN represents negative infinity
Its comparison is greater because every NaN represents positive infinity
questions.explanation: NaN represents a not-a-number case. It is unordered with numeric values, and instructions define specific flag and exception behavior for that fourth outcome.

questions.title: Do not confuse unordered with equal
questions.prompt: After a completed float comparison, the zero flag is set. Why may an equality-only check be insufficient?
options: Unordered comparison can set that flag as well as true equality
Floating-point registers store the zero flag inside every value
Every less-than result sets all comparison flags to the same state
The zero flag always describes a previous integer operation instead
questions.explanation: A completed comiss comparison with invalid masked sets ZF/PF/CF to one for unordered. ZF alone therefore cannot distinguish equality from a NaN case.

questions.title: Handle invalid order first
questions.prompt: A completed float comparison offers an unordered marker plus less/equal/greater indicators. What is a sound decision order?
options: Handle unordered first, then use ordering or equality for valid numeric cases
Handle equality first and accept it whenever its indicator is present
Handle greater first and treat every remaining value as a valid smaller number
Ignore the unordered marker because it only describes unused register bits
questions.explanation: The unordered case overlaps some equality/ordering flag tests. Handling it first prevents invalid numeric input from entering a path intended for valid ordered values.

questions.title: Use the producer's flag contract
questions.prompt: Why can signed-integer branch conditions give misleading ordering after a floating-point comparison?
options: That comparison uses a different flag contract for numeric ordering
Every floating-point comparison first converts both operands to signed integers
Signed branch conditions require the source to occupy more than one XMM register
Floating-point comparison destroys the instruction pointer before any branch runs
questions.explanation: For completed comiss, SF and OF are cleared while ZF/PF/CF encode ordering and unordered. Signed-integer ordering formulas therefore do not express this comparison's intended ordering.

questions.title: Know where arithmetic rounding comes from
questions.prompt: A scalar floating-point addition must round an inexact result. In the ordinary legacy SSE form, what controls that direction?
options: The floating-point rounding setting in MXCSR
The integer carry flag from the previous arithmetic step
The number of letters in the instruction's destination name
The last memory address used to store the player's score
questions.explanation: Ordinary scalar SSE addition and multiplication round according to MXCSR. Integer flags and register names do not choose the floating-point rounding direction.

questions.title: Keep the source available
questions.prompt: A numeric conversion reads an integer source and writes a float destination. What happens to the source in that conversion alone?
options: It keeps the integer value while the destination receives a converted value
It becomes the rounded float because every conversion rewrites both operands
It becomes zero because conversion consumes its original representation
It becomes the destination address so a later conversion can find the result
questions.explanation: The source is read, not consumed. The conversion writes its destination; the source can still be used in its original numeric representation afterward.
